screens.title: DAWs and Basic Editing
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you'll meet the Digital Audio Workstation, the software hub where you record, edit, mix, and export sounds for games. You'll learn to recognize the interface pieces you'll use every day — the timeline with tracks, the mixer with faders and inserts, and transport controls for playback. We'll also practice core edits: trimming silence, splitting clips, applying crossfades, normalizing levels, and applying basic EQ and reverb so sounds sit correctly in a game. These skills matter because game audio must be clean, consistent, and flexible; poorly prepared clips cause clicks, level jumps, or unnatural ambience that break immersion. As you follow the visual summary here, imagine importing one WAV that combines a line of dialogue and a sword clang. You'll split them, normalize the dialogue, shape the clang with EQ, and add subtle reverb to place the voice in a space. Finally you'll export a render that your game engine can use. Keep in mind a common misconception: louder always better. Instead, aim for consistent peaks, correct gain staging, and tasteful processing. Ready to explore the tools and workflow that enable clean, immersive sound in games?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › DAWs and Basic Editing
16:9 HD Classroom
Interactive overview

Understanding DAWs

A practical, tool-focused view of the workspace where game audio is shaped and prepared for engines.

In this lesson
Identify interface parts, perform fundamental edits, apply normalization, and use EQ and reverb to match game spaces.
Why it matters
Prepared audio prevents clicks, ensures consistent levels, and makes assets reusable inside a game's audio system.
Quick Orientation

Think: timeline (arrange), tracks (layers), mixer (balance), transport (playback). These are your daily tools.

Timeline & Tracks
Audio clips arranged left-to-right on tracks. Use them to layer dialogue, SFX, and music.
Mixer & FX
Faders, pan, and inserts let you shape levels and apply EQ, reverb, and other effects per track.
Transport
Playback controls and timeline navigation — essential for auditioning edits and rendering exports.
Non-destructive Editing
Edits are applied during playback or render. Originals remain safe for later adjustments.
Explore Key Topics
Editing Basics
Mixing & FX
Exporting
Start by learning how to split and crossfade clips, then normalize and lightly process sounds for consistent, game-ready assets.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives will guide your hands-on practice. First, you will identify every major DAW interface piece so you can move confidently between software. Knowing the timeline, tracks, mixer, and transport lets you find and fix audio quickly. Second, you will perform fundamental edits—trimming, splitting, and creating crossfades—so clips play cleanly and loop smoothly. These actions remove silence, isolate sounds, and prevent clicks. Third, you'll normalize audio and practice gain staging. Normalization brings peaks to a target level without changing dynamics; gain staging keeps the signal clean through processing. Finally, you'll apply basic EQ and reverb to shape tone and space, learning to use small, purposeful adjustments rather than heavy processing. Each objective includes a simple mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember the workflow and a milestone that verifies the core competency.

Interface Check

EQ & Reverb

Verification tip

Record your steps as notes or screenshots. Clear evidence of each edit helps you iterate and gives a reproducible workflow for future projects.

screens.title: What is a DAW?
screens.narratorSegment: Start by forming a clear definition. A Digital Audio Workstation is software that combines recording, timeline-based editing, mixing with faders and inserts, and export rendering into a single environment. Think of it as your virtual studio that replaces physical consoles and tape desks. In practical terms, a DAW stores references to audio files and the set of edits, effects, and automation you apply without overwriting the original files — this is non-destructive editing. For example, if you import a long WAV containing dialogue and an SFX, the DAW will remember where you split and trim clips and apply a crossfade when playing back or rendering, while leaving the original file unchanged. A common misconception is that the DAW automatically changes the file; it doesn't. That safety allows experimentation: you can normalize a copy, test different EQ curves, and undo changes at any time. Why this matters for game audio: game projects frequently reuse and repurpose assets across levels, so keeping originals intact preserves performance and flexibility. Try describing the DAW as both an editor and a project manager — it stores edits, maintains versions, and prepares final assets for export. Reflect: how will non-destructive editing change the way you experiment with sound?

keyIdea.text: A DAW is a non-destructive virtual studio combining recording, timeline editing, mixing, and export tools for preparing game audio.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › What is a DAW?
Definition & role
A DAW records, arranges, edits, processes, and renders audio without altering the original files.
Why non-destructive matters
  • Allows undo and experimentation.
  • Supports multiple versions for different in-game contexts.
  • Keeps originals intact for reuse.
Common misconception
Edits in a DAW rarely overwrite sources; they record processing and timeline edits instead.
Concrete example: splitting a combined WAV
Import a WAV with dialogue and a clang. Use the split tool to separate the two sounds, trim silence from each, and add a crossfade if they are joined. The original WAV file remains unchanged in your media folder.
Analogy: the DAW is like a photo editor that stores edit instructions rather than burning changes into the original image.
Key Takeaway
Treat the DAW as both a tool for edits and a safe place to store versions and experiment without risking originals.

screens.title: Timeline, Tracks, and Mixer
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the workspace layout is a decisive skill. The timeline is the horizontal ruler that places events in time; clips sit on it and play when their position is reached. Tracks are the horizontal lanes where you place clips; each track usually represents a single sound source or logical group, such as music, dialogue, or SFX. The mixer mirrors tracks as channels with faders, pan controls, and effect inserts. Use the mixer to control balance between tracks and to add processing that affects an entire channel. Transport controls let you audition parts and set loop points. When organizing a game asset project, keep related sounds grouped: for example, put all UI clicks on one track, footsteps on another, and ambient beds on a third. This makes global changes, like lowering all footsteps, much faster. A common error is placing unrelated sounds on the same track, which complicates mixing. Practice: import a combined file, split into two clips, move them to separate tracks, and open the mixer to add a small gain adjustment on one track. How did separating tracks change your ability to shape each sound?

keyIdea.text: Timeline arranges events; tracks isolate sources; mixer balances and inserts processing for grouped control.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Timeline, Tracks, and Mixer
Timeline: the time ruler
Marks when sounds occur. Use markers and loop regions to audition repeats and refine edits.
Tracks: lanes for sources
  • One logical element per track keeps processing targeted.
  • Group related sounds for quick global adjustments.
Mixer: balance & inserts
Faders set loudness, pan sets stereo position, inserts host EQ and reverb for the channel.
Concrete scenario
Import a WAV that has footsteps and a voiceover. Split them into two clips and place each on its own track. In the mixer, reduce the footsteps track by 2–3 dB so the voice reads clearly over the footsteps. This shows the advantage of separated tracks for fast level control.
Common mistake
Putting multiple unrelated sounds on one track forces you to apply processing that affects everything on that track, making individual fixes harder.
Key Takeaway
Organize by source and purpose: timeline positions events, tracks isolate them, mixer balances and applies processing per channel.

screens.title: Importing and Non-Destructive Editing
screens.narratorSegment: Importing audio into a DAW is simple: drag and drop or use the file import dialog. But what matters more is how edits are stored. Most DAWs perform non-destructive editing, which means the software stores edit decisions — splits, trims, fades, and effect settings — without writing those changes into the original file. For hands-on practice, import the sample WAV. Use the split tool to divide dialogue and SFX, then trim leading silence from each clip. If you want to experiment with volume, create an automation lane or adjust the track fader rather than increasing the source file gain. When you preview a crossfade or an EQ change, the DAW applies those changes in real time for playback. Because the original file is untouched, you can revert or export different variations for different game contexts. A common misconception is that export is instantaneous and overwrites originals; instead, remember to export to a new filename and format suitable for your engine. Consider naming conventions and folder structure so your non-destructive project produces easy-to-find final assets later. What folder and naming rules will you use to keep your exported assets organized?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Importing & Non-Destructive Editing
Step-by-step import
  1. Open the project and locate your media folder.
  2. Drag the WAV onto a new track or use File > Import.
  3. Name the track logically (Dialogue, SFX, Music).
Non-destructive edits explained
Edits are instruction layers. You can trim, split, and apply fades without changing the original file on disk. This enables rapid iteration and multiple exports.
Concrete example
Import game_dialogue_and_sfx.wav. Split at the dialogue end, trim silence, and add a short fade on each clip. Play back to confirm no clicks. Export a rendered WAV named edited_game_audio.wav so the original remains intact.
Common mistake
Changing source files directly instead of exporting a new file risks losing originals and reproducibility.
Pro tip
Use clear naming conventions with versions, e.g., sfx_sword_v01.wav and sfx_sword_v01_edited.wav, and keep a single export folder for engine-ready files.

screens.title: Trimming, Splitting, and Crossfades
screens.narratorSegment: These three basic edits are the foundation of clean audio. Trimming removes silence or unwanted noise at the start or end of a clip; it is often the first step after importing. Splitting slices a clip into separate items so you can rearrange or process parts independently. For instance, split a recording of several footsteps into individual hits. Crossfades blend adjacent clips so their waveforms transition smoothly. Without a crossfade, abrupt waveform discontinuities can cause clicks or pops. To create a crossfade, overlap the two clips slightly and apply a short fade curve, or use the DAW's automatic crossfade feature when joining items. Practical workflow: import the combined WAV, identify the dialogue region, split at the end, trim both clips to remove excess silence, then test playback. If you plan to loop ambient audio, create an overlap with a crossfade at the loop point to ensure a seamless repeat. A mistake to avoid is applying excessively long crossfades that alter the perceived timing of a game event; keep fades appropriate to the material. Now try splitting and crossfading a short segment to feel the difference.

keyIdea.title: Editing pattern
keyIdea.text: Trim to remove silence, split to isolate sounds, and crossfade to blend boundaries and eliminate clicks.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Trimming, Splitting, Crossfades
Trim
Shorten the start or end of a clip to remove silence or unwanted noise before the useful sound begins.
Split
Cut a clip into segments to isolate hits, dialogue lines, or phrases for targeted processing.
Crossfade
Blend adjacent clips to remove waveform discontinuities and create seamless loops or transitions.
Concrete example
From the sample file, split dialogue and the sword clang. Trim trailing silence on the dialogue. If two clips of the same ambient file are joined, overlap by 50–150 ms and apply a short crossfade to avoid any click at the seam.
Common mistake
Overlong crossfades can smear transient detail and change perceived timing — keep fades tight for percussive sounds.
Key Takeaway
Precise, minimal edits preserve character while removing artifacts; use short fades for percussive SFX and slightly longer ones for ambient material.

screens.title: Normalization and Gain Staging
screens.narratorSegment: Normalization and gain staging are distinct but related tasks. Normalization sets a clip's peak amplitude to a target level, for example -0.1 dBFS, so different files reach consistent maximum loudness. It does not compress or alter the dynamic range within the clip; it simply raises or lowers overall gain so the highest sample hits the chosen ceiling. Gain staging, in contrast, refers to setting appropriate levels at each stage of the audio chain — clip gain, track fader, bus fader, and any plugin input gains — so that processing remains clean, and clipping is avoided. In practical workflow, normalize dialogue to the chosen peak first to make it consistently audible, then use track faders to position it relative to other elements, leaving headroom on the master for any final limiting or mastering pass. A common novice error is normalizing and then boosting again without checking peaks, which can cause clipping when effects or buses add gain. As an exercise, normalize a dialogue clip to -0.1 dBFS, play it with SFX and music, and adjust track levels to leave about 6 dB of headroom on the master. What change did gain staging produce in perceived clarity?

keyIdea.text: Normalize for consistent clip peaks; gain stage to preserve headroom and avoid clipping across the mix chain.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Normalization & Gain Staging
Normalization
Adjust a clip so its loudest sample reaches a specified peak value without changing its internal dynamics.
Gain staging
Set gain at each processing stage so plugins operate with good signal-to-noise ratio and avoid clipping.
Practical rule: normalize clips first, then use track and bus faders to mix while keeping master headroom.
Example workflow
Normalize the dialogue to -0.1 dBFS. Insert SFX and music, reduce their track faders to leave ~6 dB headroom on the master. Check for clipping during heavy moments and adjust plugin gains as needed.
Common error
Normalizing everything to the same peak then summing them without headroom leads to frequent clipping on the master bus.
Key Takeaway
Use normalization for per-clip consistency and gain staging for mix-wide headroom and clean processing.

screens.title: Equalization (EQ) Basics
screens.narratorSegment: Equalization is a surgical and creative tool that changes the balance of frequency content in a sound. An EQ allows you to boost or cut specific frequency bands: lows, mids, and highs. Use EQ to remove problematic energy, such as low-frequency rumble from a weapon impact, or to enhance presence, like boosting upper mids to make a voice read clearly. Start with gentle moves — 2–4 dB adjustments — and listen critically. Avoid extreme boosts that introduce unnatural resonance. A typical workflow: apply a high-pass filter to remove subsonic rumble below 60–80 Hz for non-bass sounds, sweep a narrow bandwidth to find unpleasant frequencies and cut them, then make wide, subtle boosts to taste. A misconception is that EQ must be dramatic to work; small, targeted cuts often produce the biggest clarity improvements. Example: for a sword clang that feels muddy, cut around 200–400 Hz and slightly boost 3–6 kHz for attack. Always A/B test by bypassing the EQ to ensure the change improves the sound. What small EQ cut can you try first to unclutter a busy mix? Equalization (EQ) Basics means use eq to remove problem frequencies and make space; prefer small cuts over large boosts for clarity and natural sound.. In practical terms, shaping tone by boosting or cutting frequencies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › EQ Basics
What EQ does
Boosts or cuts specific frequency ranges to shape timbre and clarity.
Common uses
  • Remove low rumble with a high-pass filter.
  • Cut muddy mid frequencies.
  • Boost presence in upper mids for clarity.
Misconception
Large boosts are not a substitute for fixing frequency clashes; cut competing elements first.
Concrete example
A sword clang sounds muddy: apply a narrow cut around 250–400 Hz to remove boxiness, then add a tempered boost around 3–6 kHz to bring out the metallic snap. Always compare bypassed and processed versions.
Key Takeaway
EQ clears space in the frequency spectrum. Prefer thoughtful cuts and modest boosts to keep sounds natural and distinct in the mix.

screens.title: Reverb and Spatialization
screens.narratorSegment: Reverb simulates natural reflections and gives sounds a sense of environment and depth. Key parameters to understand are decay time (how long reflections last), pre-delay (time before the reflections begin), and wet/dry mix (balance of processed to original signal). Use short decay and low wet mix for close dialogue — too much reverb can push voices back and reduce intelligibility. For environmental ambience, longer decays and higher wet mixes are appropriate, but be careful not to mask important game cues. Pre-delay helps separate an initial transient from the room sound, preserving clarity while adding space. A practical approach: apply a small amount of reverb to dialogue (wet under 20%) with short decay to avoid burying the voice. For a cavernous SFX, increase decay and pre-delay to taste. A common error is using the same reverb for all assets; create different reverb sends or presets for close, mid, and far sources. When implementing in a game engine, match in-game environment reverb parameters to designer expectations so transitions feel natural. How might you adjust pre-delay to keep a sharp sword impact clear while placing it in a hall?

When implementing in a game engine, match in-game environment reverb parameters to designer expectations so transitions feel natural. keyIdea.text: Reverb adds space: tune decay, pre-delay, and wet/dry mix to place sound without sacrificing clarity; use different presets per distance category.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Reverb & Spatialization
Core parameters
  • Decay time: how long reflections last.
  • Pre-delay: time before reflections begin.
  • Wet/Dry: balance between processed and original sound.
Practical rules
Keep dialogue reverb subtle; use longer tails for ambient beds and larger spaces; use pre-delay to protect transient clarity.
Misconception
More reverb does not equal realism; it can hide detail and reduce gameplay-critical clarity if overused.
Example
For a sword impact in a hall, use moderate decay, a short pre-delay (10–30 ms) to preserve the attack, and increase wet slightly so reflections are audible but do not mask the transient.
Key Takeaway
Use reverb to match perceived distance and space while preserving the critical transient information that players rely on.

For reverb, use sends or track inserts depending on whether multiple assets share the same environment. Export settings for game audio commonly include uncompressed formats like WAV for fidelity, or compressed formats like Ogg Vorbis when budgeted for runtime size, but the key principle is to match the format and sample rate expected by the engine. Effect order & strategy
Prefer corrective EQ first, then creative processing like reverb. Use sends for shared spaces and inserts for unique coloration.

Think of export as the final handoff: deliver clean, normalized files with clear names and the correct format expected by the audio implementation team.

Gain stage

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you'll meet the Digital Audio Workstation, the software hub where you record, edit, mix, and export sounds for games. You'll learn to recognize the interface pieces you'll use every day — the timeline with tracks, the mixer with faders and inserts, and transport controls for playback. We'll also practice core edits: trimming silence, splitting clips, applying crossfades, normalizing levels, and applying basic EQ and reverb so sounds sit correctly in a game. These skills matter because game audio must be clean, consistent, and flexible; poorly prepared clips cause clicks, level jumps, or unnatural ambience that break immersion. As you follow the visual summary here, imagine importing one WAV that combines a line of dialogue and a sword clang. You'll split them, normalize the dialogue, shape the clang with EQ, and add subtle reverb to place the voice in a space. Finally you'll export a render that your game engine can use. Keep in mind a common misconception: louder always better. Instead, aim for consistent peaks, correct gain staging, and tasteful processing. Ready to explore the tools and workflow that enable clean, immersive sound in games?

These four objectives will guide your hands-on practice. First, you will identify every major DAW interface piece so you can move confidently between software. Knowing the timeline, tracks, mixer, and transport lets you find and fix audio quickly. Second, you will perform fundamental edits—trimming, splitting, and creating crossfades—so clips play cleanly and loop smoothly. These actions remove silence, isolate sounds, and prevent clicks. Third, you'll normalize audio and practice gain staging. Normalization brings peaks to a target level without changing dynamics; gain staging keeps the signal clean through processing. Finally, you'll apply basic EQ and reverb to shape tone and space, learning to use small, purposeful adjustments rather than heavy processing. Each objective includes a simple mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember the workflow and a milestone that verifies the core competency.

This second objectives page explains how to show you've learned the skills. For interface familiarity, open any DAW and point out the timeline, at least three separate tracks, and the mixer view — that proves you can locate the workspace. For basic edits, perform an import, split a combined file into dialogue and SFX, trim silence from both clips, and create a crossfade where two segments meet. For normalization and gain staging, normalize a dialogue clip to a target peak and confirm no channel clips during playback; then set track faders to leave headroom for mastering. For EQ and reverb, apply a single-band cut to remove rumble from a weapon impact and a short reverb to the dialogue with the wet/dry mix under twenty percent. Each step is small but focused. Demonstrating each action on a sample file gives you repeatable proof of competence, and this structure reduces overwhelm by breaking audio preparation into clear, verifiable steps.

Start by forming a clear definition. A Digital Audio Workstation is software that combines recording, timeline-based editing, mixing with faders and inserts, and export rendering into a single environment. Think of it as your virtual studio that replaces physical consoles and tape desks. In practical terms, a DAW stores references to audio files and the set of edits, effects, and automation you apply without overwriting the original files — this is non-destructive editing. For example, if you import a long WAV containing dialogue and an SFX, the DAW will remember where you split and trim clips and apply a crossfade when playing back or rendering, while leaving the original file unchanged. A common misconception is that the DAW automatically changes the file; it doesn't. That safety allows experimentation: you can normalize a copy, test different EQ curves, and undo changes at any time. Why this matters for game audio: game projects frequently reuse and repurpose assets across levels, so keeping originals intact preserves performance and flexibility. Try describing the DAW as both an editor and a project manager — it stores edits, maintains versions, and prepares final assets for export. Reflect: how will non-destructive editing change the way you experiment with sound?

Understanding the workspace layout is a decisive skill. The timeline is the horizontal ruler that places events in time; clips sit on it and play when their position is reached. Tracks are the horizontal lanes where you place clips; each track usually represents a single sound source or logical group, such as music, dialogue, or SFX. The mixer mirrors tracks as channels with faders, pan controls, and effect inserts. Use the mixer to control balance between tracks and to add processing that affects an entire channel. Transport controls let you audition parts and set loop points. When organizing a game asset project, keep related sounds grouped: for example, put all UI clicks on one track, footsteps on another, and ambient beds on a third. This makes global changes, like lowering all footsteps, much faster. A common error is placing unrelated sounds on the same track, which complicates mixing. Practice: import a combined file, split into two clips, move them to separate tracks, and open the mixer to add a small gain adjustment on one track. How did separating tracks change your ability to shape each sound?

Importing audio into a DAW is simple: drag and drop or use the file import dialog. But what matters more is how edits are stored. Most DAWs perform non-destructive editing, which means the software stores edit decisions — splits, trims, fades, and effect settings — without writing those changes into the original file. For hands-on practice, import the sample WAV. Use the split tool to divide dialogue and SFX, then trim leading silence from each clip. If you want to experiment with volume, create an automation lane or adjust the track fader rather than increasing the source file gain. When you preview a crossfade or an EQ change, the DAW applies those changes in real time for playback. Because the original file is untouched, you can revert or export different variations for different game contexts. A common misconception is that export is instantaneous and overwrites originals; instead, remember to export to a new filename and format suitable for your engine. Consider naming conventions and folder structure so your non-destructive project produces easy-to-find final assets later. What folder and naming rules will you use to keep your exported assets organized?

These three basic edits are the foundation of clean audio. Trimming removes silence or unwanted noise at the start or end of a clip; it is often the first step after importing. Splitting slices a clip into separate items so you can rearrange or process parts independently. For instance, split a recording of several footsteps into individual hits. Crossfades blend adjacent clips so their waveforms transition smoothly. Without a crossfade, abrupt waveform discontinuities can cause clicks or pops. To create a crossfade, overlap the two clips slightly and apply a short fade curve, or use the DAW's automatic crossfade feature when joining items. Practical workflow: import the combined WAV, identify the dialogue region, split at the end, trim both clips to remove excess silence, then test playback. If you plan to loop ambient audio, create an overlap with a crossfade at the loop point to ensure a seamless repeat. A mistake to avoid is applying excessively long crossfades that alter the perceived timing of a game event; keep fades appropriate to the material. Now try splitting and crossfading a short segment to feel the difference.

Normalization and gain staging are distinct but related tasks. Normalization sets a clip's peak amplitude to a target level, for example -0.1 dBFS, so different files reach consistent maximum loudness. It does not compress or alter the dynamic range within the clip; it simply raises or lowers overall gain so the highest sample hits the chosen ceiling. Gain staging, in contrast, refers to setting appropriate levels at each stage of the audio chain — clip gain, track fader, bus fader, and any plugin input gains — so that processing remains clean, and clipping is avoided. In practical workflow, normalize dialogue to the chosen peak first to make it consistently audible, then use track faders to position it relative to other elements, leaving headroom on the master for any final limiting or mastering pass. A common novice error is normalizing and then boosting again without checking peaks, which can cause clipping when effects or buses add gain. As an exercise, normalize a dialogue clip to -0.1 dBFS, play it with SFX and music, and adjust track levels to leave about 6 dB of headroom on the master. What change did gain staging produce in perceived clarity?

Equalization is a surgical and creative tool that changes the balance of frequency content in a sound. An EQ allows you to boost or cut specific frequency bands: lows, mids, and highs. Use EQ to remove problematic energy, such as low-frequency rumble from a weapon impact, or to enhance presence, like boosting upper mids to make a voice read clearly. Start with gentle moves — 2–4 dB adjustments — and listen critically. Avoid extreme boosts that introduce unnatural resonance. A typical workflow: apply a high-pass filter to remove subsonic rumble below 60–80 Hz for non-bass sounds, sweep a narrow bandwidth to find unpleasant frequencies and cut them, then make wide, subtle boosts to taste. A misconception is that EQ must be dramatic to work; small, targeted cuts often produce the biggest clarity improvements. Example: for a sword clang that feels muddy, cut around 200–400 Hz and slightly boost 3–6 kHz for attack. Always A/B test by bypassing the EQ to ensure the change improves the sound. What small EQ cut can you try first to unclutter a busy mix? Equalization (EQ) Basics means use eq to remove problem frequencies and make space; prefer small cuts over large boosts for clarity and natural sound.. In practical terms, shaping tone by boosting or cutting frequencies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Reverb simulates natural reflections and gives sounds a sense of environment and depth. Key parameters to understand are decay time (how long reflections last), pre-delay (time before the reflections begin), and wet/dry mix (balance of processed to original signal). Use short decay and low wet mix for close dialogue — too much reverb can push voices back and reduce intelligibility. For environmental ambience, longer decays and higher wet mixes are appropriate, but be careful not to mask important game cues. Pre-delay helps separate an initial transient from the room sound, preserving clarity while adding space. A practical approach: apply a small amount of reverb to dialogue (wet under 20%) with short decay to avoid burying the voice. For a cavernous SFX, increase decay and pre-delay to taste. A common error is using the same reverb for all assets; create different reverb sends or presets for close, mid, and far sources. When implementing in a game engine, match in-game environment reverb parameters to designer expectations so transitions feel natural. How might you adjust pre-delay to keep a sharp sword impact clear while placing it in a hall?

After edits and level setup, apply effects thoughtfully and export a final file suitable for your engine. Typical order: clean up with EQ, add spatial effects like reverb, and then check final levels. When using EQ, make surgical cuts first, then gentle boosts for presence. For reverb, use sends or track inserts depending on whether multiple assets share the same environment. Before exporting, confirm normalization and headroom: the master bus should not exceed your intended maximum peaks. Export settings for game audio commonly include uncompressed formats like WAV for fidelity, or compressed formats like Ogg Vorbis when budgeted for runtime size, but the key principle is to match the format and sample rate expected by the engine. Name exported files clearly and place them in an engine-ready folder. A common mistake is forgetting to bounce stems when the engine expects separate SFX and dialogue files. For practice, apply EQ to the clang, add a subtle reverb to the dialogue, then export two files: one for dialogue and one for the SFX. How will you name and organize these exported assets so they are ready for the audio implementation pipeline?
